sentences.text: The genus Ptychotherates is monotypic, known only from the species Ptychotherates bucculentus, which is represented by a partial skull.
The holotype preserves a nearly complete but somewhat disarticulated skull, providing most of the cranial material for study.
Its generic name combines Greek roots meaning “fold” and “hunter,” reflecting an interpretation of its anatomy.
The specific epithet bucculentus translates as “with full cheeks,” a reference to its unusually tall jugal bone.
The jugal bone of Ptychotherates is taller and deeper than that of any other known Triassic dinosaur, giving it the appearance of full cheeks.
Fossils of Ptychotherates were uncovered in 1982 at the Coelophysis Quarry in Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
The holotype specimen is curated at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under accession number CM 31368.
Ptychotherates shares derived features (synapomorphies) with Tawa hallae, such as distinctive depressions on the quadrate and otoccipital bones and a dorsoventrally tall, laterally flat jugal.
It is set apart from other contemporary ornithodirans by possessing the proportionally deepest jugal known for any Triassic dinosaur.
Within Morphoraptora, it is closely allied with Chindesaurus, Daemonosaurus and Tawa, forming a subgroup of early herrerasaurian dinosaurs.
The animal lived in the Late Triassic, specifically during the Norian or Rhaetian ages.
Its remains come from the Chinle Formation at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, United States.
The age of the deposits is estimated between 205.7 and 201.4 million years ago, corresponding to the Rhaetian stage.
